en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Section on the Puzzling Questions, Chapter on Omniscient Knowledge.
8. The Question of Queen Amarā “Venerable Nāgasena, this was said by the Blessed One:
‘If one should obtain a moment or a private opportunity...’”
“Or even if one were to obtain such a Nimantaka;
would all women commit evil,
having found no other [partner] than a cripple?”

Furthermore, it is said: “The wife of Mahosadha, a woman named Amarā, while staying in a village with her husband away on a journey, sat in private and secluded; though she made her husband equal to a king and was invited with a thousand pieces of gold, she did not commit evil.
If, venerable Nāgasena, it was spoken by the Blessed One: “If...
[and so forth]...”
“As for the statement, ‘Indeed, [it is so]! Therefore, “Mahosadha’s wife...
did not do it,” that is false.
If Mahosadha’s wife... [did it].”
“Since he did not do so, then that statement of yours—‘If... together with’—is also false.
This too is a double-pronged question that has come to you; it must be resolved by you.”
“Great King, this was indeed spoken by the Blessed One: ‘If...
together with...’”
And it is said: “The wife of Mahosadha … [omission] … did not do so.
Great King, would that woman, even if she were offered a thousand [pieces of gold], commit an evil deed with such a man?
She would not have done so had she found such an opportunity, a place of secrecy, or even an instigator;
yet, O Great King, as that immortal woman reflected, she saw no opportunity, no place of secrecy, nor any such instigator.
In this world, out of fear of censure, she saw no opportunity; in the next world, out of fear of hell, she saw no opportunity, for the ripening of the fruit is bitter.

She did not see the opportune moment because of her evil deeds; she did not see the opportune moment because she was unwilling to let go of what was dear to her; she did not see the opportune moment because of her excessive devotion to her husband;
she did not see the opportune moment because she failed to honor the Dhamma; she did not see the opportune moment because she censured the ignoble;
she did not see the opportune moment because she was unwilling to break her habitual conduct.
For many such reasons, she did not find a moment [to commit evil].
Even when she was alone, having searched the world and finding no opportunity, she did not do evil.
Had she found privacy from humans, she would not have found privacy from non-humans.
If one were to find seclusion from non-human beings, one would not find seclusion from those who have gone forth and possess knowledge of the minds of others.
If one were to find seclusion from those who have gone forth and possess knowledge of the minds of others, one would not find seclusion from deities who possess knowledge of the minds of others.
If one were to find seclusion from deities who possess knowledge of the minds of others, one would not find seclusion even from one’s own evil deeds.
If she could have obtained secrecy through her own wickedness, then she would not have obtained secrecy through unrighteousness.
Not having obtained secrecy through such various means as these, she did not commit evil.
Even though she searched the world for an instigator, failing to find anyone of that sort, she did not commit evil.
"Mahosadha, Great King, is a wise man endowed with twenty-eight qualities.
With which twenty-eight qualities is he endowed?
Mahosadha, Great King, is brave, modest, conscientious, has a following, is possessed of friends, is patient, virtuous, and truthful."
Endowed with purity, free from anger, without arrogance, not envious, energetic, industrious, inclusive, generous, gentle, humble in conduct,
mild, honest, without guile, possessed of great intelligence, renowned, accomplished in knowledge,
seeking the welfare of those who depend on him, desired by all people, wealthy, and famous.
“Great King, the wise Mahosadha was endowed with these twenty-eight qualities.
Since she could not find another suitor like him, she did not commit that evil deed.
“Excellent, Bhante Nāgasena! It is so; I accept it as you have said.”
The eighth question: The Question of Amarādevī.
